listeningScripts.title: Booking a Bulky Waste Collection
listeningScripts.text:
Officer: Good morning, Harewood Council, waste services.
Caller: Hello — I need to get rid of an old sofa and a fridge. I believe you collect.
Officer: We do. Can I take your name?
Caller: It's Constance Ilesanmi. Ilesanmi is I-L-E-S-A-N-M-I.
Officer: And your address?
Caller: Fifty-two Beckford Terrace.
Officer: A contact number?
Caller: 07920 447 813.
Officer: Now, the fridge has to be recorded separately from the sofa. Anything with a cooling system is handled under different rules because of the gas inside it, so it goes on a separate vehicle.
Caller: Does that cost more?
Officer: It does. The standard charge is twenty pounds for up to three items, and a fridge or freezer is fifteen pounds on its own. So thirty-five in total for what you've described.
Caller: Fine. When can you come?
Officer: The next slot is the twenty-seventh of February. Collections are between seven in the morning and three in the afternoon, and I'm afraid we can't narrow it beyond that.
Caller: Do I need to be there?
Officer: No, and most people aren't. But the items must be outside, at the front, accessible from the pavement by eight — crews will not enter a property or a rear garden, and a collection they cannot reach is charged as if it happened.
Caller: Understood. Anything else about the sofa?
Officer: Yes, and this catches people. It must have the fire safety label still attached. Without it we cannot take it, because it goes for reuse if it's in good condition, and no label means it cannot be resold.
Caller: I'll check tonight.
Officer: Please do. If the label is missing, ring back and I'll change the booking to disposal rather than collection for reuse, which is the same price but a different vehicle.
Caller: How do I pay?
Officer: Card over the phone now, or online within forty-eight hours, otherwise the slot is released.
Caller: I'll pay now.

listeningScripts.title: Science Centre Explainer Induction
listeningScripts.text:
Coordinator: Welcome, everyone, and thank you for volunteering as weekend explainers at the Calder Science Centre. I'm Rina, and I run the explainer programme.

Let me be clear about the job, because it is not demonstrating. An explainer's work is to notice a visitor who is stuck or bored, approach them, and ask a question — not to deliver a talk. The commonest mistake new explainers make is explaining. You will be tempted to tell a child how the exhibit works; the better move is to ask what they think will happen if they press the other button.

Shifts are Saturday and Sunday, four hours, and we ask for two shifts a month. Under-sixteens can volunteer with us but only alongside a named adult volunteer, which is a safeguarding requirement rather than a judgement about capability.

Training is one full day, and it covers the exhibits, safeguarding, and what to do in an evacuation. There is a refresher every six months which is not optional, because exhibits change and the ones that break change more often.

Now the building. Coming through the main doors, the ticket desk is on your right. The main gallery, which is where most explainers work, is straight ahead through the arch and takes up the whole ground floor beyond it. The workshop room, used for booked school sessions, is on the left of the ticket desk. Upstairs, the planetarium is directly above the main gallery, and the café is at the front of that upper floor, overlooking the entrance. The explainer room, where you sign in and leave your things, is behind the ticket desk and is the one place in the building where you can sit down out of sight of visitors.

Finally, something worth hearing plainly. If you do not know the answer to a question, say so and find out together. Children are entirely unbothered by an adult who doesn't know something and very quick to spot one who is pretending.

listeningScripts.title: Confidentiality in a Placement Report
listeningScripts.text:
Tutor: Right — the placement report. You were at the engineering firm, weren't you?
Marcus: Yes, six months in their testing department.
Tutor: And the difficulty?
Marcus: A lot of what I did is commercially confidential. I signed something on the first day.
Tutor: Good that you've raised it now rather than after writing forty pages. Have you read what you signed?
Marcus: Not carefully.
Tutor: Then that is the first job, because these agreements vary enormously. Some prohibit naming clients; some prohibit describing processes; a few prohibit saying which projects existed at all.
Marcus: What if it's the strict kind?
Tutor: Then you write the report at one level of abstraction higher. "A component was tested against a customer specification" rather than naming the customer or the component. The assessment is on what you learned and how you worked, not on the technical details of their product.
Marcus: Won't that make it vague?
Tutor: It makes the subject matter vague and the reflection specific, which is the right way round for this assessment. A report that says exactly what you found difficult, what you tried, and what you would do differently is strong even if the object is described generically.
Marcus: Should I ask the company?
Tutor: Yes, and ask a named person, in writing, and keep the reply. "My supervisor confirmed by email that this level of detail is acceptable" protects you and them. Do not rely on a corridor conversation.
Marcus: What about the appendix? I have data.
Tutor: If in doubt, leave it out. An appendix is where confidential material usually escapes, because people paste in a spreadsheet they have stopped looking at closely.
Marcus: And if they refuse permission entirely?
Tutor: Then tell me immediately and we adjust the assessment. That has happened before and it is a solvable problem, provided it surfaces in March rather than in June.

listeningScripts.title: Why Things Are Hard to Repair
listeningScripts.text:
Lecturer: Today I want to look at why so many manufactured objects are difficult or impossible to repair, and to argue that the usual explanation — deliberate sabotage by manufacturers — is both too simple and not needed to explain what we observe.

Start with the design decisions themselves. Gluing a case together rather than using screws is cheaper, faster on the production line, and produces a thinner, better-sealed product. Soldering a battery to a board removes a connector that could fail and saves space. Each of these is defensible on its own terms, and each also makes repair difficult. The unrepairable object is usually the accumulated by-product of decisions taken for other reasons.

Where intent enters is subtler and better documented. Restricting who may buy spare parts, refusing to publish service manuals, and using software checks that reject a genuine replacement component fitted by an independent workshop — these are not consequences of engineering choices. They are commercial policies, and they are what repair legislation has generally targeted, correctly.

Economics does much of the remaining work. As manufacturing costs fell, the labour cost of a repair rose relative to the price of a replacement, so a repair that takes an hour becomes irrational against an item costing little more. That calculation is real, and it is also incomplete, because it prices the labour and not the materials, the energy or the disposal.

The legislation that has followed is more modest than its coverage suggests. Requirements to supply parts for a stated number of years, to publish repair documentation, and to design for disassembly do address the commercial barriers. They do not change the labour arithmetic, and the evidence so far is of a real but limited increase in repair rather than a transformation.

I want to end on what the evidence actually supports, because this is a subject where confident claims outrun it. Products genuinely have become harder to repair; the dominant cause is a combination of design priorities and labour economics rather than a plan; the deliberate obstruction that does exist is concentrated in parts and information rather than in the hardware; and the interventions with the best evidence behind them are the dull ones — parts availability, published manuals, and removing the software locks.
